questions.stem: What makes a disease non-infectious?
options: It is caused by a pathogen that cannot survive outside the human body
It is caused by a pathogen that spreads only through insect vectors
It is caused by a pathogen that has been weakened by vaccination
It is not caused by a pathogen and cannot pass from person to person
questions.explanation: Non-infectious diseases arise from genetic, environmental, nutritional or lifestyle causes rather than pathogens, so they are not transmitted between people. Diseases spread by vectors are infectious.

questions.stem: Which disease is caused mainly by a nutritional deficiency?
options: Cystic fibrosis
Mesothelioma
Huntington's disease
Scurvy
questions.explanation: Scurvy results from a lack of vitamin C, which is needed to make collagen, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing. Cystic fibrosis and Huntington's disease are genetic, and mesothelioma is caused by asbestos.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a non-infectious disease and its main cause is correct?
options: Mesothelioma: inhaling asbestos fibres
Cystic fibrosis: a diet low in protein
Rickets: an inherited faulty CFTR allele
Goitre: long exposure to UV radiation
questions.explanation: Mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining of the lungs, is caused by inhaled asbestos fibres, an environmental cause. Cystic fibrosis is caused by faulty CFTR alleles, rickets by a lack of vitamin D or calcium, and goitre by a lack of iodine.

questions.stem: Type 2 diabetes is more common in people with a family history of it, and also in people who are physically inactive and overweight. What does this show?
options: Both genetic and environmental factors affect the risk of the disease
It is caused only by inherited alleles, and lifestyle plays little part
It is an infectious disease that spreads between members of a household
It is caused only by diet, and the family link is from sharing meals
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is multifactorial: inherited variants raise susceptibility, and inactivity, diet and excess weight add to the risk. It is not caused by a pathogen.

questions.stem: Why did Australia make it mandatory to use iodised salt in bread?
options: To prevent iodine deficiency, which impairs thyroid function
To reduce folate deficiency, which causes neural tube defects in babies
To reduce sodium intake and so lower the population's blood pressure
To reduce tooth decay, which is common in children and older adults
questions.explanation: Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones, and deficiency can cause goitre and impair brain development before birth and in childhood. Adding it to a staple food reaches most of the population; folic acid fortification targets neural tube defects.

questions.stem: Mandatory fortification of bread-making flour with folic acid aims to reduce which condition?
options: Goitre caused by a lack of iodine
Scurvy caused by a lack of vitamin C
Rickets caused by a lack of vitamin D
Neural tube defects such as spina bifida
questions.explanation: Low folate around conception and in early pregnancy increases the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Goitre is prevented by iodine and scurvy by vitamin C.

questions.stem: The Slip! Slop! Slap! campaign, launched in Victoria in 1981, aimed to prevent which disease?
options: Heart disease, by encouraging less salt
Skin cancer, by encouraging sun protection
Lung cancer, by encouraging smokers to quit
Type 2 diabetes, by encouraging exercise
questions.explanation: The campaign urged people to slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen and slap on a hat to reduce UV exposure, the main environmental cause of skin cancer in Australia. It was followed by the SunSmart program.

questions.stem: A state runs a sun-protection campaign for ten years. Which evidence would best show that the campaign reduced skin cancer?
options: A rise in the number of people who report having seen the campaign's advertisements
Higher sales of sunscreen in the month the campaign's television advertisements began
A survey showing that most people could remember and liked the campaign's slogan
A sustained fall in melanoma incidence among younger age groups, compared with before
questions.explanation: The aim is fewer cases, so the best measure is a lasting change in the disease rate itself, especially in the younger people whose sun exposure the campaign changed. Awareness, sunscreen sales and recall of the slogan show reach, not a health outcome.

questions.stem: After plain packaging of tobacco was introduced in Australia, smoking rates kept falling. Why is it difficult to measure how much of the fall plain packaging caused?
options: Smokers are deliberately left out of the national health surveys that measure smoking
Smoking rates in a population can be estimated only once in every twenty years
Other measures, such as tax rises, and an existing downward trend acted at the same time
Every country in the world introduced plain packaging in the very same year as Australia
questions.explanation: When several interventions overlap and rates were already falling, the effect of one measure is confounded with the others, so researchers need comparison data and statistical models. Australia was the first country to introduce plain packaging.

questions.stem: What is epidemiology?
options: The treatment of individual patients who have an infectious disease
The study of the structure and cells of the human immune system
The study of the distribution and causes of disease in populations
The study of how pathogens damage the cells of one patient
questions.explanation: Epidemiology looks at who gets a disease, where and when, and why, across whole populations, to guide public health and disease control. It applies to non-infectious as well as infectious diseases.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes an experimental epidemiological study from an observational one?
options: The researchers record what happens without intervening in any way
The researchers study only people who already have the disease
The researchers use only data collected from past hospital records
The researchers assign the exposure or treatment
questions.explanation: In an experimental study, such as a randomised clinical trial, the researchers decide who receives the intervention. In observational studies they record exposures and outcomes as they occur.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes an analytical epidemiological study?
options: It describes who has a disease, where and when, without testing a cause
It assigns a new treatment at random to groups of volunteers
It reports one unusual patient in detail for other doctors
It compares groups to test a hypothesis about a cause of a disease
questions.explanation: Analytical studies, such as cohort and case-control studies, compare exposed and unexposed groups, or cases and controls, to test whether a factor is linked to disease. Describing patterns without testing a cause is descriptive, and assigning treatment is experimental.

questions.stem: Researchers recruit 10,000 healthy adults, record how much each person exercises, and follow them for 20 years to see who develops heart disease. What type of study is this?
options: Cross-sectional study
Randomised clinical trial
Case study
Cohort study
questions.explanation: A cohort study follows a group forward in time, comparing outcomes in people with different exposures. In a randomised trial the researchers would assign the amount of exercise.

questions.stem: A survey measures the blood pressure and salt intake of 2,000 adults on a single occasion. What type of study is this?
options: Case study
Cross-sectional study
Cohort study
Randomised clinical trial
questions.explanation: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at the same point in time, like a snapshot. It can show an association but not which came first, unlike a cohort study.

questions.stem: A doctor publishes a detailed report on one patient with an unusual reaction to a new medicine. What type of study is this, and what is its main limitation?
options: A cohort study; it follows far too many patients to report in detail
A cross-sectional study; it measures the patient only one time
A clinical trial; it has no placebo group to compare against
A case study; one patient cannot show how common the reaction is
questions.explanation: A case study describes a single patient or a few patients and can flag a new problem, but it cannot measure frequency or establish cause. Cohort studies follow large groups over time.

questions.stem: Why are participants in a randomised clinical trial allocated to groups at random?
options: So the trial can be run without any control group for comparison
So other factors are spread evenly between groups, reducing selection bias
So each participant can choose the treatment they would prefer to receive
So the researchers can put the sickest people into the treatment group
questions.explanation: Random allocation means that age, health and other factors, including unknown ones, are likely to be similar in each group, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. Letting people or researchers choose introduces selection bias.

questions.stem: In a double-blind trial of a new drug, who knows which participants receive the drug and which receive the placebo?
options: Both the participants and the researchers assessing them
Neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them
Only the participants, not the researchers assessing them
Only the researchers assessing them, not the participants
questions.explanation: Double-blinding prevents expectations from influencing the results: participants cannot show a placebo effect based on knowing their group, and assessors cannot be biased in recording outcomes.

questions.stem: Why is the link between smoking and lung cancer studied with cohort and case-control studies rather than a randomised trial?
options: Smoking has too small an effect to detect in a trial
It would be unethical to assign people to smoke
Randomised trials test only drugs, not behaviours
Cohort studies are always more accurate than trials
questions.explanation: Randomly assigning people to a known harmful exposure would breach research ethics, so observational studies are used. Randomised trials can test behaviours such as diet or exercise programs.

questions.stem: Which is an example of disease surveillance used to manage disease in Australia?
options: Hospitals treat their patients without keeping records of the diagnoses they make
Vaccines are given to the community only after an outbreak has been declared
Doctors and laboratories must notify health departments of cases of certain diseases
Patients decide for themselves whether to tell anyone about a positive test result
questions.explanation: Notifiable disease reporting gives health departments continuous data on cases, so outbreaks can be detected and responded to quickly. Surveillance depends on systematic collection of data, not individual choice.

questions.stem: Health authorities test sewage for fragments of a virus's genetic material. What is an advantage of this surveillance method?
options: It detects infection in a whole community, even in untested people
It identifies exactly which person in the community has the infection
It measures how severe the illness is in each infected person
It removes the need for any testing of patients in clinics
questions.explanation: Wastewater testing picks up virus shed by everyone connected to the sewer, including people with no symptoms, so it gives an early warning of rising infection. It cannot identify or assess individuals, so clinical testing is still needed.

questions.stem: Which term describes the number of new cases of a disease in a population over a set period?
options: Morbidity
Mortality
Incidence
Prevalence
questions.explanation: Incidence counts new cases over a period, such as a year. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point in time, both new and old.

questions.stem: What does the prevalence of a disease measure?
options: The number of people who die from the disease each year
The proportion of patients with the disease who recover
The proportion of people who have the disease at one time
The number of new cases of the disease that arise over a year
questions.explanation: Prevalence includes everyone who currently has the disease, however long they have had it. New cases over a period are the incidence, and deaths are the mortality.

questions.stem: What is the difference between morbidity and mortality?
options: Morbidity applies to infectious diseases; mortality to the rest
Morbidity is illness from a disease; mortality is death from it
Morbidity is death from a disease; mortality is illness from it
Morbidity is new cases of a disease; mortality is existing cases
questions.explanation: Morbidity describes the burden of illness, such as how many people are sick or disabled by a disease, while mortality describes deaths. Both terms apply to any disease.

questions.stem: A town of 20,000 people records 50 new cases of a disease in one year. What is the incidence rate per 100,000 people per year?
questions.explanation: Incidence rate = 50 / 20,000 x 100,000 = 250 per 100,000 per year. The answer 50 is the raw count, not a rate.

questions.stem: A new treatment keeps people with an incurable disease alive much longer but does not cure them. If the number of new cases each year stays the same, what happens over time?
options: Prevalence falls while incidence rises
Prevalence rises while incidence stays the same
Incidence rises while prevalence stays the same
Both prevalence and incidence fall over time
questions.explanation: Incidence depends only on new cases, which are unchanged; prevalence counts everyone living with the disease, and people now live with it for longer, so it rises. Prevalence is roughly incidence multiplied by how long the disease lasts.

questions.stem: Diseases X and Y each have an incidence of 5 per 100,000 per year. The prevalence of X is 2 per 100,000 and of Y is 100 per 100,000. Which explanation best fits these data?
options: Y kills its patients more quickly than X does
Y lasts years; X is brief or quickly fatal
Y has many more new cases each year than X has
X is an infectious disease and Y is non-infectious
questions.explanation: With equal incidence, higher prevalence means each case lasts longer, as in a chronic disease people live with for years. Faster death would lower prevalence, not raise it.

questions.stem: In one year, a country of 5 million people has 2,000 cases of a disease and 100 deaths from it. What is the mortality rate per 100,000 people?
questions.explanation: Mortality rate = 100 deaths / 5,000,000 x 100,000 = 2 per 100,000. The figure 5 is the percentage of cases who died (100 / 2,000), and 40 is the number of cases per 100,000.

questions.stem: In 1854, John Snow mapped cholera deaths in London and found they clustered around one water pump in Broad Street. How did this information help control the outbreak?
options: It led to residents being given a newly developed cholera vaccine
It showed that cholera spread in the air, so windows were sealed
It pointed to contaminated water, so the pump's handle was removed
It identified the cholera bacterium under a light microscope
questions.explanation: The pattern of cases implicated the pump as the source, and removing its handle cut off that supply, even before the cholera bacterium was widely recognised. This is an early example of epidemiological data guiding disease control.

questions.stem: Which scientist is correctly matched with work that underpins modern disease management?
options: Rita Levi-Montalcini: discovery of transposable elements in maize
Rosalind Franklin: development of the first vaccine against polio
Rosalyn Sussman Yalow: radioimmunoassay to measure hormones in blood
Barbara McClintock: discovery of nerve growth factor in animal cells
questions.explanation: Yalow developed radioimmunoassay, which measures tiny amounts of hormones such as insulin. McClintock discovered transposable elements, Levi-Montalcini discovered nerve growth factor, and Franklin's X-ray images revealed the structure of DNA.

questions.stem: Two variables in a study are correlated. What does this mean?
options: They change together, but one does not necessarily cause the other
One variable always causes the change seen in the other variable
They were measured using the same equipment in the same study
One variable was controlled while the other was kept constant
questions.explanation: A correlation is a pattern in which two variables rise or fall together. It may be causal, but it can also be due to chance or to a third factor linked to both.

questions.stem: Ice cream sales and cases of sunburn both rise in summer. What is the best explanation for the correlation?
options: Both are linked to a third factor, hot sunny weather
Eating ice cream makes the skin more sensitive to the sun
Sunburn makes people more likely to buy ice cream
The correlation proves a causal link between them
questions.explanation: Hot, sunny days increase both ice cream sales and UV exposure, so weather is a confounding factor. A correlation alone never proves causation.

questions.stem: Early studies found women with cervical cancer more often had antibodies to herpes simplex virus 2. Later, HPV DNA was found in nearly all cervical cancers, and HPV proteins were shown to disrupt control of cell division. What do these findings show?
options: Neither virus is linked to cervical cancer, which is purely an inherited disease
HPV causes cervical cancer; the herpes link was a correlation, as both spread sexually
Herpes simplex virus causes cervical cancer, and HPV infects the tumours afterwards
Both viruses cause cervical cancer equally, so the herpes link is also causal
questions.explanation: HPV is found consistently in the tumours and has a known mechanism for causing cancer, which supports causation. Herpes infection is associated with cervical cancer because both are spread by sexual contact, a shared risk factor, not because herpes causes it.

questions.stem: Since HPV vaccination began in Australia, rates of precancerous cervical abnormalities in young women have fallen sharply. Why does this support HPV as a cause of cervical cancer?
options: It shows that cervical cancer is mostly an inherited disease
It shows that HPV and cervical cancer are only correlated
Preventing the suspected cause reduced the disease
It shows that the vaccine kills cancer cells directly in the cervix
questions.explanation: If HPV causes cervical cancer, preventing infection should reduce the disease, and this is what has been observed. The vaccine prevents infection; it does not treat existing cancer.

questions.stem: Which set of evidence most strongly supports a causal link between asbestos exposure and mesothelioma?
options: Risk rises with dose, exposure comes before disease, and many studies agree
Most mesothelioma patients are older men who live in large cities
One study found more mesothelioma among people living near a mine
Asbestos use and mesothelioma both increased in the twentieth century
questions.explanation: A dose-response relationship, the right order in time and consistent results across studies are strong criteria for causation. A single study or two trends that rise together could be due to chance or confounding.

questions.stem: In a study of coffee drinking and heart disease, coffee drinkers were also more likely to smoke. Why is smoking a problem for this study?
options: It is a placebo effect experienced by the participants who drank coffee
It is a confounding factor linked to both coffee drinking and heart disease
It is the independent variable that the researchers chose to investigate
It is a measurement error caused by faulty equipment in the study
questions.explanation: Smoking is associated with coffee drinking and independently causes heart disease, so it could create or exaggerate an apparent link between coffee and heart disease. Researchers must control for it.

questions.stem: How can researchers reduce selection bias when choosing participants for an epidemiological study?
options: Let the researchers choose people who seem likely to show an effect
Select participants at random from the whole population being studied
Choose the volunteers who respond first to a newspaper advertisement
Recruit all of the participants from a single specialist hospital clinic
questions.explanation: Random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of inclusion, so the sample represents it. Volunteers and patients of one clinic differ systematically from the general population.

questions.stem: Which approach reduces the effect of confounding factors in a case-control study?
options: Increasing the number of cases while adding no controls to the study
Asking participants to guess which group they have been placed in
Measuring the outcome only in the cases and not in the controls
Matching each case with a control of similar age, sex and smoking status
questions.explanation: Matching makes cases and controls similar in factors that could otherwise explain a difference, so the exposure being studied is the main difference between them. Controls are essential for any comparison.

questions.stem: Early in a pandemic, reported cases rose sharply in the week that testing became far more widely available. What does this show about the data?
options: Testing caused the infection to spread faster that week
Part of the rise may reflect more testing, not more infection
The pathogen must have mutated into a more infectious strain
The case numbers reported before that week were accurate
questions.explanation: Reported cases depend on how many people are tested, so a change in testing introduces measurement bias; earlier figures were probably underestimates. A mutation might also raise cases, but the timing points to testing.

questions.stem: In a study, people with a disease are asked about their diet ten years earlier, and they recall it in more detail than healthy controls. What type of bias is this?
options: Selection bias, from how people were chosen
Confounding, from an unmeasured third variable
Random error, from a small sample size
Recall bias, a form of information bias
questions.explanation: People with a disease often search their memory harder for possible causes, so the information collected differs in accuracy between groups. This is recall bias, a type of information bias, not a problem with how participants were selected.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of people taking part in large epidemiological studies?
options: The studies remove the need for any medical treatment in future
The results apply only to the participants themselves and not to others
The data reveal risk factors and guide prevention for everyone
Every participant is guaranteed to avoid the disease being studied
questions.explanation: Large studies give the statistical power to detect risk factors and evaluate interventions, and their findings shape public health programs for everyone. Taking part does not protect the individual participant.
